おぼえた ばかり の こもりうた — The lullaby just learned

You say “nothing but, all the time…” (～ばかり, ～て ばかり いる) and “I've just…, recently” (～た ばかり), and you tell ～た ばかり apart from ～た ところ; in the spring when Rosa Elena does nothing but sleep and cry, and Mihai finally learns Haruka's lullaby correctly.
nursemaid, the one who looks after a child

To use noun + ばかり (“nothing but…, all…”, with a sense of excess or reproach) and tell it apart from だけ and しか ～ない.
To say that someone does nothing but something: ～て ばかり いる / ～て ばかり だ.
To say you did something recently: ～た ばかり, ～た ばかり の + noun, ～た ばかり な のに / だ から.
To choose correctly between ～た ばかり (recently, as it feels to you) and ～た ところ (just now, as an exact moment).
A Sunday in mid-March, 9:00 in Bucharest, 16:00 in Hiroshima. Haruka promised to teach Mihai the correct lullaby (ch. 46). Sakura is sitting by the piano. Rosa Elena, in Ana's arms, is whimpering.
Mihai, are you ready? Today I'll teach you all the correct lyrics.
Please do. I just kept listening to the CD over and over and had no idea what it meant.
(Laughing) How's Hana-chan? Is she sleeping well?
Lately she either sleeps nonstop or cries nonstop. She smiles only a tiny bit.
All newborn babies are like that. Sakura, too, did nothing but cry.
That's not true! I did nothing but laugh, right?
At night you did nothing but cry. In the daytime you did nothing but sleep. And because of that, Mom was always short on sleep.
Then let's begin. “Hush-a-bye, go to sleep, little one. The little boy is a good child, now go to sleep.”
Yes. But I used to sing “Sakura is a good child” to her. You can sing “Hana-chan is a good child”.
Next: “Where has the little boy's nursemaid gone? Over that mountain, back to her village she's gone.” “Omori” is the person who looks after a baby. “Sato” means one's home village.
Yes. In the old days, young girls looked after children and sang this song. That's why it's a little sad.
And at the end: “What present did she bring you from her village? A little bead drum and a flute.”
This! (She shows a toy to the camera and twirls it) It's from when I was a baby.
(Singing slowly) Hush-a-bye, go to sleep, little one. Hana-chan is a good child, now go to sleep…
Mihai, it's all correct! Well done!
I've only just learned it, so I'm not confident yet. Maybe I'll have forgotten it by tomorrow.
If you forget it, I'll teach you again! But no “I'll get angry”!
(Softly) See how well it works? This song has been putting babies to sleep for more than a hundred years.

ba-ka-ri: three even syllables. In speech, especially when you complain, it becomes ばっかり (ba-k-ka-ri): っ is a tiny pause before “ka” that stresses the word — “nothing but, nothing but”.
bō-ya: long “o”, hold it for two syllables (bo-o-ya). よいこ (yo-i-ko): three short syllables, no long “o”. In the song, each syllable gets its own note.
ma-n-ka-i: ん before “k” is pronounced at the back of the mouth, like the “n” in “anchor”. ha-na-bi-ra: four even syllables, with a light tapped “r”.
1. Noun + ばかり: “nothing but…, all…” (and rather too much)

ばかり after a noun means “only this, this everywhere”. Unlike だけ (a neutral limit, “only”), ばかり almost always carries a sense of EXCESS or REPROACH: “nothing but this, and it's too much”. In English: “nothing but…”, “all…”, “constantly…”.
and that's not good, I should eat something else too
I didn't eat anything but bread.
little, less than I should have
All around were nothing but strangers. (ch. 24)
everywhere, as far as the eye could see
ばかり takes the place of が and を: パン を ばかり ✗ → パン ばかり ✓. Other particles usually stay in front of it: こども に ばかり やさしい (“is kind only to children”), スマホ で ばかり あそぶ.
In everyday speech you'll very often hear ばっかり (with っ). Haruka uses it for emphasis: よる は ないて ばっかり. It's the same form, just more expressive.
2. ～て ばかり いる: “to do nothing but…”

The ～て form + ばかり いる = someone keeps doing the same thing and nothing else. Most often it's a complaint or an amused observation. In the past: ～て ばかり いた. It can also be shortened with だ: ないて ばかり だ / だった.
I just kept listening to the CD and didn't understand the meaning.
Stop playing all the time and get studying!
Watch the word order: ばかり goes between ～て and いる. ✗ ないて いる ばかり → ✓ ないて ばかり いる. (ないて いる ばかり does exist, but it's rarer and literary: “could do nothing but cry”.)
Past-tense verb + ばかり = the action happened RECENTLY. Important: “recently” as the speaker FEELS it. It can be a few minutes, but also two months or a year, if it still feels new to you.
I've only just gone back to work.

Useful forms: ～た ばかり の + noun (かった ばかり の もんだいしゅう = the workbook I just bought); ～た ばかり な のに (“even though I've just…”: おぼえた ばかり な のに、もう きかない); ～た ばかり だ から (“because I've just…”: いま おぼえた ばかり だ から、じしん が ない). As with ところ, before のに you add な.
4. ～た ばかり or ～た ところ?
In ch. 46 you learned ～た ところ (“have just…”). Both are often translated as “just”, but they're not the same:
the exact moment: it has just this second finished
the feeling that it's still new, recent
minutes… months, as it feels to you
With きのう / せんげつ
いま ねた ところ。(she has just this moment fallen asleep)
うまれた ばかり。(she was born recently)

When it's a matter of a few moments, both usually work: いま おぼえた ところ / いま おぼえた ばかり. The difference: ところ answers “at what point are you?”, while ばかり usually adds a consequence (“…so I don't know it well yet / so it's strange that…”).
ばかり after a verb in the DICTIONARY form or ～て has a different meaning (nothing but / constantly): ないて ばかり = cries nonstop; ないた ばかり = has just cried. Always look at the form of the verb!
“ねんねん ころりよ” (江戸子守唄, the lullaby from Edo, old Tokyo) is the best-known lullaby in Japan. It has a few old-fashioned forms:
(ころり = to tumble softly, to drop off to sleep)

In the old days, in families with many children, young girls, sometimes still children themselves, were hired as nursemaids (こもり, おもり). They carried the baby on their back and sang to it — that's why many Japanese lullabies are a little sad: they talk about homesickness and the home village (さと).

でんでん だいこ is an old toy: a little drum on a stick, with two beads tied on strings. When you twist the stick, the beads hit the drum: “den-den”. You can still buy one today, for example at the stalls near temples in Japan.

たなか しゃちょう から の メール — Mr Tanaka's email
Around 25 March, Mihai gets an email from Mr Tanaka (ch. 36–37). The new device for the ward, from Hikari Medical, has arrived in Bucharest.
Dear Mr Mihai, once again, congratulations on the birth of your daughter.
The new device arrived at the hospital in Bucharest only yesterday. The manual you so kindly translated arrived along with it.
I shall come to see you next Monday.
I imagine you have only just returned to work and are very busy. Please do not overexert yourself.
My granddaughter, Hinata, does nothing but look at photos of your daughter lately. She has entrusted me with a letter, which I shall bring you.

みっつ の こもりうた — Three lullabies
Even in March, Rosa Elena's day didn't change much.
She drinks, sleeps, cries and drinks again. Days of nothing but sleeping and nothing but crying.
And Ana's day, too, was nothing but milk and nappies. When she looked in the mirror, she had dark circles under her eyes.
“Lately I've been eating nothing but bread.”
Elena, who had come over at lunchtime, heard this and went straight into the kitchen: “Nothing but bread won't do! Here, ciorbă.”
Mrs Doina next door often brought them food, too. “It's fine for a baby to do nothing but cry. Crying is how they grow.”
The food Mrs Doina brought was, for some reason, always sarmale.
Mr Petre from upstairs laughed: “In the old days my dog kept you all from sleeping. Now we're even.”
At the two-month check-up, Rosa Elena had reached five kilos.
When they said they were worried that she cried nonstop, the paediatrician laughed: “It's a sign that she's healthy.”
8 March is Women's Day in Romania.
On his way home from work, Mihai bought three bunches of flowers: for Ana, for Elena and for Mrs Doina.
“And for Rosa Elena?” Ana asked, and Mihai took a small tulip out of his pocket and put it next to the cot.
But Rosa Elena wasn't interested in flowers: she did nothing but sleep.
In Mihai's bag there was also a Japanese workbook he had just bought: a book for the N4 exam.
That evening, Mihai only opened the first page and fell asleep with his head on the book.
From then on he decided to do a little at a time after Rosa Elena fell asleep. But he was so sleepy he did nothing but yawn, and he hardly made any progress.
After learning the correct lyrics from Haruka in mid-March, Mihai sang the song every evening.
Since it was a song he had only just learned, he glanced at his notebook now and then as he sang.
Haruka had said: “When you understand the lyrics, the song changes.” And sure enough, since he understood what he was singing, Mihai's singing had become gentler.
Strangely enough, when Mihai sang “Hana-chan is a good child”, Rosa Elena usually calmed down right away.
One evening, though, it was different. No matter how many times he sang, Rosa Elena wouldn't stop crying.
“But I'm singing it correctly… I've only just learned it, and it already doesn't work anymore?”
Ana took over and held her, and softly sang her a Spanish lullaby that Carmen used to sing to her long ago.
And Rosa Elena fell asleep in the blink of an eye.
“…So she likes Mom's song better,” said Mihai, a little put out.
Ana laughed: “She must have been in a Spanish mood today. Tomorrow she might want a Romanian song.”
So Mihai decided to remember and also sing the Romanian lullaby that Elena used to sing to him long ago.
The next day, Elena heard it and, without saying a word, gazed at Mihai's face for a long time. Then she took off her glasses and wiped her eyes.
“That's the song from when you were a baby, and yet you remembered it. You cried nonstop too, and only when I sang you this song would you finally fall asleep.”
Ana called Carmen, asked her for all the lyrics of the Spanish lullaby and wrote them in the notebook. Now the notebook held songs in Japanese, Romanian and Spanish, side by side.
And so Rosa Elena's nights filled up with lullabies from three countries.
At the end of March, company president Tanaka came to Bucharest again: the new device had just arrived at the hospital.
The manual Mihai had translated was neatly placed next to the device.
In front of the device, the president and Dr Ionescu shook hands firmly.
“Mr Mihai, you've only just returned to work, you must be tired,” the president said kindly.
Mihai answered, “No, I'm fine,” but right at that moment a huge yawn escaped him.
The president laughed and took an envelope out of his bag: “It's from my granddaughter, Hinata.”
Inside was a drawing of a sunflower and a baby. In the corner, in small letters, it said: “Thank you for the postcard from Spain.”
That evening, Ana stuck the drawing on the wall, next to the lullaby notebook.
The next day a parcel arrived from Hiroshima. Inside was Sakura's bead drum. When Mihai twirled it while singing, Rosa Elena's eyes went wide.
One Sunday at the beginning of April, the three of them went out for the first time for a longer walk, with the stroller.
Their destination: the Japanese garden in Herăstrău Park.
The cherry trees had only just started to bloom. Under the pink blossoms there was a little bridge and stone lanterns too.
A Japanese family had spread out a blanket and was eating obentō.
In the pond, some big koi carp were opening and closing their mouths.
“Who'd have thought we could go cherry-blossom viewing in Bucharest!” Ana said happily.
When Mihai made a video call, Sakura shouted from the other side of the screen: “There are cherry trees in Bucharest too?!”
“The cherry trees in Hiroshima are in full bloom right now too. We're enjoying the blossoms on the same day as Hana-chan!”
Rosa Elena, from the stroller, stared at the flowers she was seeing for the first time.
Then, in the warm spring sunshine, she fell asleep again.
And Sakura, on the other side of the screen, pouted: “Hana-chan, nothing but sleeping again!”
Maybe she heard Sakura's voice, because Rosa Elena opened her eyes a little and closed them again.
Little Hana-chan, who still does nothing but sleep and cry. But when they looked at her sleeping face, both their tiredness just vanished.
Pushing the stroller, Mihai sang softly: “Hush-a-bye, go to sleep, little one. Hana-chan is a good child, now go to sleep.”
A cherry petal fell onto Rosa Elena's little cheek.
Ana gently picked it up and pressed it between the pages of the lullaby notebook.
“Mihai, she's only just been born, but one day I'd like us to show her the cherry blossoms in Kyoto too.”
“The cherry trees at Mrs Fumiko's teahouse. We'll definitely go and see them.”

ばかり: nothing but, constantly, just
ばかり or ところ? Translate
Translate into Japanese (kana or romaji). Think: is it an exact moment or “recently”?
She has just fallen asleep (this very moment).
In the evening, after the singing lesson, Sakura (9) writes in her diary.
15 March, sunny. Today we taught big brother the correct lyrics of the lullaby. Mom taught him, but I was the one who played the piano.
This week I practised nothing but the lullaby. I didn't play any other pieces at all.
Even though he had only just learned it, big brother sang it well. And Hana-chan fell asleep right away. That kind of bugs me.
Mom says: “You, too, did nothing but cry back then.” But I don't remember.
I've decided to give my bead drum to Hana-chan. I'm a big sister now, so I don't need it anymore. Tomorrow Mom and I will take it to the post office.
